messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: IT Support
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Amina is a 43-year-old African American woman who works in IT support for a large medical office and came to treatment after years of carrying a private sense of danger and defectiveness that she had never fully spoken aloud. She is married and, by her account, outwardly dependable and composed, the person at work who can usually troubleshoot under pressure. What she described in the first sessions, however, began much earlier, in childhood, in episodes of physical abuse by a caregiver that took place in conditions that still feel vividly present to her. When she thinks of what happened, she does not remember it as a single abstract fact from the past. She remembers being shut into a small room and the feeling of having nowhere to go. She remembers the particular terror of hearing a lock and knowing she was contained with no way out. She also remembers being taken into a natural area where no one else was around, the kind of setting that should have felt open but instead felt exposed and unsafe. Even now, what stands out to her is not only the pain but the certainty she had as a child that she had somehow brought it on, that there must have been something in her that made an adult treat her that way.

As she grew older, Amina did not set these experiences aside so much as organize her life around not coming too close to them. Talking directly about what happened has always felt dangerous to her. If a conversation edges toward childhood or abuse, she notices her whole body tighten before she has even decided what to say. She becomes acutely aware of her shoulders, jaw, and stomach, as if she is bracing for impact. She said that even when she knows, logically, that she is sitting with her husband or in a therapist’s office, her body can react as though something bad is about to happen. The same thing occurs in enclosed spaces. If a conference room door closes during a staff meeting, especially if the room is small and windowless, she feels a rush of alarm that seems out of proportion to the moment, but to her it does not feel false at all. Her attention shifts immediately to the door, to whether it is locked, to how quickly she could leave. She has sometimes missed parts of meetings because she is tracking the room rather than what her coworkers are saying.

Her work in IT support confronts her with this more often than she would like. She is frequently called into cramped server closets or small locked offices to fix printers, terminals, or network equipment. She has developed quiet habits that make sense to her: leaving doors slightly ajar when she can, positioning herself nearest the exit, asking practical-sounding questions that allow her to delay going into certain rooms. These strategies have not gone unnoticed. She worries that colleagues see her as difficult or distracted. On days when she is already tense, she finds it hard to concentrate on troubleshooting steps she knows well, and then that lapse itself becomes proof, in her mind, that something is wrong with her.

The same pattern appears outside work. Her husband enjoys hiking and weekend drives, but Amina has gradually withdrawn from outings in wooded parks or isolated natural areas. She does not describe nature as generally unpleasant; rather, certain settings abruptly feel too similar to where some of the abuse occurred. The sight of trees closing in around a trail, the feeling of being away from other people, can make her body surge into readiness before she can talk herself down. She then feels ashamed, because she believes other people would simply enjoy the scenery, whereas she experiences it as threat. Over time she has come to speak about herself in harsh, global terms. She has said she must be the kind of person these things happen to, that there is something defective in her character, not just something painful in her past. These beliefs are not fleeting thoughts for her; they are the explanations she has carried for years.

What brought her now was a recent combination of strain at work and increasing distance at home. After becoming overwhelmed in a closed office while trying to repair a computer, she had to step out abruptly and could not easily explain why. Around the same time, she turned down another outing with her husband rather than risk ending up somewhere that felt too much like before. He urged her to get help, not because he doubted her strength, but because he could see how much effort it took for her to get through ordinary days. Amina arrived to treatment frightened of what would happen if she spoke in detail, certain that revisiting the past might make her lose control, but also quietly hoping that she might no longer have to live as if danger were always one door, one conversation, or one stretch of trees away.
